job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Victor Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Norrby, in the room over the garage where my dad keeps his plumbing van. I'm up by seven, I work out, and then I'm calling or messaging tradesmen: plumbers, sparkies, roofers, guys my dad knows. I'm building a little service that does their quotes, invoices and tax paperwork using AI tools, so they can stay on site. Afternoons I do applications as well, because I haven't ruled out a proper firm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what were your internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Accounting and finance, top of my year. One internship was at a regional building supplier, Haldane Timber, in accounts receivable, chasing late payers, which taught me how people dodge invoices. The other was at a small accountancy practice that does tax for the self-employed. Both showed me that tradesmen hate paperwork and pay well to avoid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because hype that doesn't deliver is just noise. I already use the tools every day and they help me, but they're not magic. I'd tell the lads that they're a better spanner, not a replacement for the plumber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay but not comfortable. I have debt, about two months saved and no offer, and a small business that's not big enough to live on yet. A quiet AI world means a slow market, which is hard on a start-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the business: sign up five more tradesmen, build a simple monthly package, and ask my first clients to recommend me. I'd keep applying to accountancy firms, since a second option is smart. And I'd put away a fixed amount from every client payment before I spend a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly impatient. I want it to be moving faster. When I feel it, I go for a run or do a hundred more phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many clients do you have so far, and what do they pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four so far, paying between sixty and a hundred and twenty a month each. It's not much, about three hundred in total, but it comes every month. If I get to twenty clients, I can live on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father think about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's proud, but he's a bit of a sceptic. He says paperwork is a waste of a good plumber, so he gets why people would pay. He lets me use the van office, and he gave me my first two clients.

say: I'd say it's a **better spanner**, not a replacement for the plumber.
I'd tell the lads that hype that doesn't deliver is **just noise**.

fieldNote: Victor treats the plain-AI world as a **slow market** for his start-up, not a threat.
He has real if tiny revenue and a plan to reach twenty clients.

steps.text: Sign five more tradesmen for the monthly paperwork package
Keep applying to accountancy firms as a second option
Put aside a fixed amount from every client payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's good for people who work. Tools do the paperwork, and the person who understands the customer wins. I'd tell the lads: don't fight it, use it, and pay a young guy to set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit uneasy, because the tools that make my service possible could also let tradesmen do it themselves. My edge would be trust and setup, not the software. It's a race to be the one they ring first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the client list to fifteen and add services like quarterly tax estimates and late-payment chasing. I'd learn a couple more tools and build my own templates, so I'm quicker than anyone. And I'd invest a little in a better laptop and a proper website, since it pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with an edge. It's a bit like the start of a match, where you're nervous but you know the game. I like that more than waiting around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your business when everyone can do this with a tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most will use it to do their own invoices, and some will do it badly. My value is the quarterly review, the chasing and the phone call when something goes wrong. If I keep a human voice, I can keep clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the firms you apply to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd hire fewer juniors, I'd say, so I'd treat the accountancy applications as a backup. If an offer came, I'd think about doing both, a job in the day and the business on weekends. A firm that lets me do that gets a better employee.

say: I'd say it's good for **people who work**, so don't fight it, use it.
I'd tell the lads to pay a young guy to **set it up**.
think: The tools that make my service possible could also let tradesmen do it **themselves**.
My edge would be **trust and setup**, not the software.

fieldNote: Victor's thinking is **entrepreneurial**: his edge is trust and service, not software.

steps.text: Grow to fifteen clients with quarterly tax estimates and late-payment chasing

Buy a better laptop and a proper website for the business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the right response is to move quickly, not wait for help. People should keep working, look after their families and keep an eye on their neighbours. I'd say governments should stay out of the way and still keep the basics running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be rattled. In two years even my service could be done by a tool in the hand of every tradesman. I'd be asking if the whole idea of accounting as a job is ending, and I'd be asking it at twenty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at the business and try to sign thirty clients in a year, since small firms will still want someone they know. I'd cut costs to the bone and put every spare pound into savings. I'd also learn a trade skill with my father on weekends, because hands matter longer than screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit wired. It's the sort of news that makes me want to move, not sit. But I'd be lying if I said I wasn't scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Dad, you were right to teach me to work with my hands too. I'd ask him to teach me plumbing basics on weekends, and he'd laugh and say about time. He'd tell me to keep the business too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the business survive if everyone's using tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because customers will still want to talk to someone they trust, who knows their job and their van. The more AI there is, the more a person on the phone stands out. But I can't promise it, and I'd say so.

I'd say governments should keep the **basics running** and stay out of the way.
think: I'd be **rattled**, because in two years even my service could be done by a tool in every tradesman's hand.
I'd be asking whether **accounting** is ending as a job, at twenty-three.

feel: **Anxious**, and a bit wired, wanting to move rather than sit.
S2.quote: The more AI there is, the more a person on the phone stands out.
fieldNote: Victor's reaction is **action first**: move, build, save, learn a trade skill.

He is honest that his bet on trust could fail.

steps.text: Sign thirty small-firm clients within a year

Learn plumbing basics from my father at weekends
Take any steady accounts job that pays if the business stalls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is what you make of it. People who start building now will be fine, and those who wait for permission won't. I'd say it's a chance for people who work hard, and the government should keep taxes low for small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but pumped. I could build the business, hire someone, and get a second revenue line, like helping tradesmen with the AI side of their quotes. I'd need to be ahead of the curve the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work toward fifty clients and hire a part-timer to handle the phones. I'd put money into a van-load of tools for a side trade, perhaps a small property or a share portfolio, because I want income that isn't dependent on me. I'd also join the local business group at church and the chamber of commerce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charged up, and a little worried. It's the one I'd choose if I had to, because I'd get time to build and test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you build in the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty clients, a part-timer and a name people recognise locally. I'd like to be the person the tradesmen in three towns call when they're drowning in paperwork. That's a decent business, and it could survive a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about being self-employed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Income that disappears when I'm ill, and no safety net. I've got my parents, which helps, but I don't want to need them. So I'd keep a six-month reserve and pay into a pension, even if it's only a little.

say: I'd say five years is **what you make** of it, so start building now.
I'd say government should keep **taxes low** for small firms.
think: I'd be **anxious but pumped**, with time to build and hire someone.
I'd need to be **ahead of the curve** the whole way.

S3.quote: I'd like to be the person the tradesmen in three towns call when they're drowning in paperwork.
fieldNote: Five years suits Victor's **builder** mindset: clients, staff, a name.
He worries about income stopping when he's ill and plans a reserve.
Joining the chamber of commerce fits his community and business instincts.

steps.text: Grow to fifty clients and hire a part-timer for the phones

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time to build something that lasts, so people should get on with it. Work hard, be honest, and don't wait for someone to fix it. And I'd say we should look after those who struggle, through family and community first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly fine. I could build a proper company, marry, and buy a house. I'd stay alert, because the business would need to change a few times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business to a proper small firm with staff, and qualify as an accountant so I can sign things. I'd buy a flat as an investment and move out of the room above the garage. I'd also keep learning each new tool as it arrives, since that's how I stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit smug if I'm honest. It's the world where my plan works the way I imagine, which is a nice thing to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm with ten people, a wife, a house and a place at church. I'd like to employ some of the graduates who can't find work now. That feels like the right use of luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The market could shrink faster than I think, or a big software company could offer tradesmen the same service free. If that happened, I'd go into advisory work. I'd rather be early to react than proud.

I'd say we should look after the **struggling** through family and community first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no doubt. Two years is too quick for anyone to build a business that survives, and I'd be starting from nothing in a crowded market. What would help is low taxes and rules for new small firms, a bit of public backing for people starting up, and customers who still want a person they can call.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a nervous person, and I still feel it. People expect me to say I'm fine because I'm good with tools, and that isn't the whole story. I'd rather build something than wait for a company to pick me.

headlineQuote: I'd rather build something than wait for a company to pick me.
portrait: **Victor** is a 23-year-old accounting graduate, top of his class, living with his parents above his father's plumbing van garage.
He is **traditional and pro-market**, values family and work, and uses AI tools every day.
He builds a paperwork service for **tradesmen**, using his father's contacts and his own receivables experience.
He moves first in every scenario: **side income**, investing, and a business, while still applying for a proper firm.
His mood is uneasy or anxious by speed, and calm only with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, because two years is too quick to build a business that survives in a crowded market.
whatWouldHelp: **Low taxes** and light rules for new small firms, plus some public backing for people starting up.
Customers who still want a **person they can call**.
